newsitem.title: USA: House votes to lift U.S. tuna embargo.
newsitem.headline: House votes to lift U.S. tuna embargo.

text.p: Fishing fleets could kill as many as 5,000 dolphins a year in nets and still keep their dolphin-safe certification on some tuna under legislation passed on Wednesday by the House of Representatives.

The House voted 262-166 for legislation the White House pushed as a way to put into law changes Mexico and other countries that fish the Eastern Tropical Pacific agreed to make in their tuna fishing methods.
The Clinton administration and congressional backers of the bill say granting those countries access to the U.S. market again would keep them from returning to more dolphin-deadly methods.

The bill sets a cap of 5,000 allowable dolphin deaths annually. It also allows cans of tuna caught in the encircling nets to bear the "dolphin-safe" label as long as shipboard observers did not see any dolphins killed.

However, the bill faces tougher sledding in the Senate, where Democrats Barbara Boxer of California and Joseph Biden of Delaware have said they would move to block it. They stopped the bill in the Senate last year after the House approved it.

Opponents said the bill would sanction fishing methods in which dolphins were encircled, harassed, injured and possibly killed. They also said the White House was bowing to pressure from Mexico, which threatened to challenge the embargo in the World Trade Organisation.
"It is designed to head off a contentious encounter with Mexico, whose fishing fleet would rather not contend with dolphins when hauling in tuna," Michigan Democrat David Bonior said.

But bill sponsor Wayne Gilchrest, a Maryland Republican, said: "This is about protecting dolphins in the Eastern Tropical Pacific Ocean with an international agreement. This has nothing to do with us giving up sovereignity."

Hundreds of thousands of dolphins used to be killed in the eastern Pacific where they tend to swim above schools of tuna. Fishing vessels placed huge encircling nets to trap the fish, drowning dolphins in the process.

To push the United States to lift the embargo it imposed in response to the dolphin slaughter, fishing countries including Mexico and Venezuela have reduced deaths to about 3,000 annually through more cautious methods, although they still set encircling nets on dolphins.
